```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
```

## Data

We use the GUSTO-I trial data that ships with the package. The outcome is
30-day mortality (`day30`). We split it into a development sample, used only to
fit the models, and a validation sample, used to evaluate them.

```{r data}
library(voipred)

set.seed(1)
i   <- sample(nrow(gusto))
dev <- gusto[i[1:5000], ]
val <- gusto[i[5001:10000], ]

mean(val$day30)   # prevalence in the validation sample
```

A small function to draw the decision curve from the result of `nb()`:

```{r plot-fun}
plot_nb <- function(res, main) {
  plot(res$threshold, res$NB_model, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#2a78d6",
       ylim = c(-0.01, max(res$NB_all)), xlab = "Risk threshold",
       ylab = "Net benefit", main = main)
  lines(res$threshold, res$NB_all, lwd = 2, col = "#eb6834", lty = 2)
  abline(h = 0, lwd = 2)
  legend("topright", c("Model", "Treat all", "Treat none"), lwd = 2,
         col = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "black"), lty = c(1, 2, 1), bty = "n")
}
```

## Example 1: logistic regression

```{r glm}
fit_glm <- glm(day30 ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse + pmi + miloc + sex,
               family = binomial, data = dev)

res_glm <- nb(fit_glm, data = val, outcome = "day30",
              thresholds = seq(0, 0.30, by = 0.01))
head(res_glm, 8)
```

The result is a data frame with one row per threshold:

- `NB_model`: net benefit of treating patients whose predicted risk is at or
  above the threshold,
- `NB_all`: net benefit of treating everyone,
- `NB_none`: net benefit of treating no one (always 0).

```{r plot-glm}
plot_nb(res_glm, "Logistic regression")
```

## Example 2: random forest

For a `ranger` forest, it must be a probability forest (`probability = TRUE`);
a forest that only predicts classes is rejected.

```{r rf}
fit_rf <- ranger::ranger(factor(day30) ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse + pmi + miloc + sex,
                         data = dev, probability = TRUE, num.trees = 500, seed = 1)

res_rf <- nb(fit_rf, data = val, outcome = "day30",
             thresholds = seq(0, 0.30, by = 0.01))
plot_nb(res_rf, "Random forest")
```

## Example 3: Bayesian logistic regression (bayespred)

A `bpmfit` model from bayespred. The risk is the posterior mean of risk.

```{r bpm}
library(bayespred)
fit_bpm <- bpmfit(day30 ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse + pmi + miloc + sex,
                  data = dev, prior = log_f(m = 2))

res_bpm <- nb(fit_bpm, data = val, outcome = "day30",
              thresholds = seq(0, 0.30, by = 0.01))
plot_nb(res_bpm, "Bayesian logistic regression (bayespred)")
```

## Options

| Argument | What it does |
|---|---|
| `model` | A fitted model that gives predicted probabilities (see "Models tested" below). A vector of predicted risks is not accepted. |
| `data` | The validation sample. It must contain every covariate the model was developed with. |
| `outcome` | The binary outcome: a column name (`"day30"`), or a vector with one value per row. The event is 1: 0/1, logical (TRUE = 1), or a two-level factor. |
| `thresholds` | Risk thresholds in [0, 1). Default `seq(0, 0.99, by = 0.01)`. |
| `weights` | Optional observation weights, e.g. sampling weights. |
| `predict_function` | Optional `function(model, newdata, ...)` returning the predicted risks. Works for any model (see "Any other model" below). |

**How the risks are obtained.** voipred keeps no list of supported models. It
uses, in this order: your `predict_function` if given; a `predict_risk()` method for
the model's class if there is one; otherwise the standard routes,
`predict(model, newdata, type = "response")`, then `type = "prob"`, then
`riskRegression::predictRisk()`. voipred ships `predict_risk()` methods only
for the models these standard routes cannot handle (`svm`, `naiveBayes`,
`nnet`, `lda`/`qda`, `glmnet`, `xgb.train()`, LightGBM, CatBoost). Whatever the
route, the result must be probabilities, as checked below.

**Models tested.** For each of the following models, the test suite checks on
GUSTO-I that `nb()` gives the same net benefit as `dcurves::dca()` (model,
treat all and treat none) at every threshold from 0 to 0.99, and all pass:

| Type | Models |
|---|---|
| Regression | `glm` (logit, probit and cloglog links), Firth logistic regression (`logistf`), `mgcv::gam`, MARS (`earth` with a binomial glm) |
| bayespred | Bayesian logistic regression (`bpmfit`, and its `posterior()` object), risk = posterior mean of risk |
| Trees and ensembles | `rpart`, `partykit::ctree`, `ranger` (`probability = TRUE`), `randomForest`, `gbm` |
| Other machine learning | k-nearest neighbours (`kknn`), naive Bayes (`naivebayes`, `e1071::naiveBayes`), support vector machine (`e1071::svm`, `probability = TRUE`), neural network (`nnet`), `MASS::lda`, `MASS::qda` |
| Trained on a numeric matrix | `glmnet` (one lambda), `cv.glmnet`, XGBoost (`xgb.train` and `xgboost()`), LightGBM, CatBoost |

Models trained on a numeric matrix need the validation data to have columns
with the same names as the training matrix (e.g. dummy columns such as
`KillipII`); `xgboost()` and CatBoost also accept factors directly.

**Any other model.** If none of the routes works for a model, `nb()` says so
and asks for `predict_function`, a function that returns the risks. For example,
for an SVM (which voipred also handles by itself):

```{r predict-fun}
fit_svm <- e1071::svm(factor(day30) ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse, data = dev,
                      probability = TRUE)
vars <- c("age", "Killip", "sysbp", "pulse")
nb(fit_svm, val, "day30", thresholds = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2),
   predict_function = function(model, newdata, ...) {
     # predict.svm drops rows with missing values in any column, so pass
     # only the model's covariates
     pr <- predict(model, newdata[, vars], probability = TRUE)
     attr(pr, "probabilities")[, "1"]
   })
```

The author of a modelling package can instead add one `predict_risk()` method
for their model class; `nb()` then works with it without `predict_function`.

**Missing covariates.** If the validation data lacks a covariate the model was
developed with, `nb()` stops and names it:

```{r missing, error = TRUE}
nb(fit_glm, val[, setdiff(names(val), c("sysbp", "pulse"))], "day30")
```

**Labels instead of probabilities.** A model that only predicts the class
(0 or 1) cannot be used. For example, a `ranger` forest fitted without
`probability = TRUE` has no route to probabilities, and the message says how
to refit it:

```{r labels, error = TRUE}
fit_class <- ranger::ranger(factor(day30) ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse,
                            data = dev, num.trees = 100, seed = 1)
nb(fit_class, val, "day30")
```

Any model whose predictions are only 0s and 1s is stopped with a message that
they look like predicted classes (labels).

**Scores instead of probabilities.** Values below 0 or above 1 are not
probabilities. They may be wrong, or scores from the model that must first be
turned into probabilities. For example, a linear regression fitted to the 0/1
outcome gives some negative predictions:

```{r scores, error = TRUE}
fit_lm <- lm(day30 ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse, data = dev)
nb(fit_lm, val, "day30")
```

The test suite checks that this error is raised for: a linear regression on
the 0/1 outcome, log-odds from `glm`, `glmnet` and `gbm` (their default
`predict()` scale), XGBoost raw scores (`binary:logitraw`), LightGBM raw
scores, CatBoost raw values (`RawFormulaVal`), SVM decision values and LDA
discriminant scores. Predicted classes are stopped in the same way, as shown
above; this is tested for `ranger` and `svm` fitted without
`probability = TRUE`, and for class predictions from `rpart`, naive Bayes and
CatBoost.

**Ties.** As in `dcurves`, a patient is treated when the predicted risk is at
or above the threshold, and a predicted risk of exactly 0 is never treated.
The test suite checks that `nb()` reproduces `dcurves::dca()` for logistic
regression, two random forest packages and bayespred.

## Weights: one bootstrap draw

`nb()` also accepts observation weights. Besides sampling weights, this is how
bootstrap draws of the net benefit are made, without copying the data:

- **Ordinary bootstrap:** the weight of each patient is the number of times
  they are drawn when sampling `n` patients with replacement.
- **Bayesian bootstrap:** the weights follow a Dirichlet(1, ..., 1)
  distribution, drawn as independent exponential(1) values divided by their
  sum.

```{r bootstrap}
n <- nrow(val)
z <- c(0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20)

set.seed(2)
w_boot <- tabulate(sample(n, replace = TRUE), nbins = n)   # ordinary bootstrap
w_bb   <- rexp(n)
w_bb   <- n * w_bb / sum(w_bb)                              # Bayesian bootstrap (Dirichlet)

draws <- rbind(
  original           = nb(fit_glm, val, "day30", z)$NB_model,
  ordinary_bootstrap = nb(fit_glm, val, "day30", z, weights = w_boot)$NB_model,
  bayesian_bootstrap = nb(fit_glm, val, "day30", z, weights = w_bb)$NB_model)
colnames(draws) <- paste("z =", z)
round(draws, 4)
```

The ordinary-bootstrap weights give exactly the same result as resampling the
rows:

```{r bootstrap-check}
idx <- rep(seq_len(n), w_boot)
all.equal(nb(fit_glm, val[idx, ], "day30", z)$NB_model,
          unname(draws["ordinary_bootstrap", ]))
```

Repeating such draws many times gives the uncertainty in net benefit that the
next steps of voipred use for ΔNB, P(useful), P(best) and EVPI.
